title: De Consensu Evangelistarum
author: Augustine
source: Translated by Claude from stoa0040.stoa037.opp-lat1, as held by Open Greek and Latin's CSEL.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.

passages.original: Socrates autem, quem rursus in actiua, qua mores informantur, omnibus praetulerunt, ita ut testimonio quoque dei sui Apollinis omnium sapientissimum pronuntiatum esse non taceant, Aesopi fabulas pauculis uersibus persecutus est uerba et numeros suos adhibens rebus alterius, usque adeo nihil scribere uoluit, ut hoc se coactum imperio sui demonis fecisse dixerit, sicut nobilissimus discipulorum eius Plato commemorat, in quo tamen opere maluit alienas quam suas exornare sententias. quid igitur causae est, cur de istis hoc credant, quod de illis discipuli eorum litteris commendarunt, et de Christo nolint credere, quod eius de illo discipuli conscripserunt, praesertim cum ab eo ceteros homines sapientia superatos esse fateantur, quamuis eum fateri deum nolint?
passages.english: Socrates, moreover, whom they in turn ranked above all in the active [part of philosophy], by which morals are shaped, so that they do not keep silent that he was even declared by the testimony of their god Apollo to be the wisest of all, put some of Aesop's fables into a few verses, applying his own words and metres to another man's matter, and he was so unwilling to write anything that he said he had done this under compulsion, by the command of his *daimōn* [guiding spirit], as Plato, the most famous of his disciples, records; and yet in that work he preferred to adorn the ideas of another rather than his own. What reason is there, then, why they should believe of these men what their disciples committed to writing about them, and yet refuse to believe of Christ what his disciples wrote about him, especially since they admit that all other men were surpassed by him in wisdom, although they refuse to admit that he is God?

passages.original: Quid quod isti uani Christi laudatores et christianae religionis obliqui obtrectatores propterea non audent blasphemare Christum, quia quidam philosophi eorum, sicut in libris suis Porphyrius Siculus prodit, consuluerunt deos suos, quid de Christo responderent, illi autem oraculis suis Christum laudare * conpulsi sunt? nec mirum, cum et in euangelio legamus eum demones fuisse confessos; scriptum est autem in prophetis nostris: quoniam di gentium demonia. ac per hoc isti, ne contra deorum suorum responsa conentur, continent blasphemias a Christo et eas in discipulos eius effundunt;
passages.english: What of the fact that these empty praisers of Christ and oblique detractors of the Christian religion do not dare to blaspheme Christ for this reason, that certain of their philosophers, as Porphyry the Sicilian reports in his books, consulted their gods as to what they should answer about Christ, and those [gods] were compelled by their oracles to praise Christ? Nor is this surprising, since we also read in the gospel that the demons confessed him; and it is written in our prophets: "For the gods of the nations are demons." And for this reason these men, so as not to strive against the responses of their gods, hold back their blasphemies from Christ and pour them out upon his disciples;
passages.notes: The asterisk after 'laudare' is an editorial mark in the source, possibly indicating a textual problem; it was omitted. The quotation is Psalm 95(96):5.

passages.original: si enim di sunt, quorum uates consulti ab hominibus ut non dicam fefellerunt, proxima tamen priuatis negotiis responderunt, quomodo non est deus, cuius uates non solum ea, quae ad tempus consulebantur, congrue responderunt, uerum etiam unde non consulebantur de uniuerso genere humano adque omnibus gentibus ea tanto ante. praedixerunt, quae nunc et legimus et uidemus? si deum dicunt, quo impleta Sibylla fata cecinit Romanorum, quomodo non est deus, qui et Romanos et omnes nationes in se unum deum per Christi euangelium credituras et omnia patrum suorum simulacra euersuras, sicut praenuntiauit, exhibuit?
passages.english: For if they are gods whose seers, when consulted by men, answered things close to their private affairs, not to say that they deceived them, how is he not God whose seers not only answered fittingly the things they were consulted about for the time being, but also, where they were not consulted, foretold so long beforehand concerning the whole human race and all nations the things which we now both read and see? If they call him a god by whom the Sibyl was filled when she sang the fates of the Romans, how is he not God who, just as he foretold, has shown that both the Romans and all nations would believe in him as the one God through the gospel of Christ and would overthrow all the images of their fathers?

passages.original: Istae, inquiunt, fabulae sunt aut interpretandae a sapientibus aut ridendae; nos autem Iouem colimus, de quo ait Maro: Iouis i s omnia plena, id est omnia uiuificantem spiritum. merito ergo et Varro Iouem opinatus est coli a Iudaeis, quia dicit per prophetam: caelum et terram ego impleo. quid illud quod idem poeta dicit aethera?
passages.english: "These," they say, "are fables, either to be interpreted by the wise or to be laughed at; but we worship Jupiter, of whom Maro says: 'All things are full of Jupiter,' that is, the spirit that gives life to all things." With good reason, then, did Varro too suppose that Jupiter was worshipped by the Jews, since [God] says through the prophet: "I fill heaven and earth." What about that which the same poet calls the ether?
passages.notes: 'Iouis i s omnia plena' is a scanning split of 'Iovis is omnia plena'... read as 'Iovis omnia plena' (Virgil, Eclogues 3.60). Maro is Virgil. The prophet quoted is Jeremiah 23:24.

passages.original: quid igitur mirum est, si hoc fecerunt antiquiores homines de Ioue et Saturno et ceteris, quod Romani de Romulo, quod denique iam recentioribus temporibus etiam de Caesare facere uoluerunt? quibus et Vergilius adulationem carminis addidit dicens: ecce Dionaei processit Caesaris astrum. uideant ergo, ne forte historica ueritas sepulchra falsorum deorum ostendat in terra, uanitas autem poetica stellas eorum non figat, sed fingat in caelo. neque enim re uera stella illa Iouis est aut illa Saturni;
passages.english: What wonder is it, then, if the men of older times did with Jupiter and Saturn and the rest what the Romans did with Romulus, and what finally, in more recent times, they wished to do even with Caesar? To these Virgil also added the flattery of his verse, saying: "Behold, the star of Dionaean Caesar has come forth." Let them see to it, then, that historical truth does not perhaps show the tombs of false gods on earth, while poetic vanity does not fix their stars in heaven but fabricates them. For in truth that star is not Jupiter's, nor that one Saturn's;
passages.notes: Wordplay in the Latin: 'non figat, sed fingat' (does not fix, but feigns/fabricates). 'Dionaean' refers to Caesar's descent from Venus, daughter of Dione (Virgil, Eclogues 9.47).

passages.original: uiderunt, quam esset absurdum, si filius temporis Iuppiter haberetur, quem deum aeternum uel putabant uel putari uolebant. at uero secundum istam nouellam interpretationem, quam ueteres eorum si habuissent, mirum si Ciceronem Varronemque latuisset, Saturni filium Iouem dicunt tamquam ab illa summa mente profluentem spiritum, quam uolunt esse uelut animam mundi huius omnia caelestia et terrena corpora implentem. unde illud Maronis est, quod paulo ante commemoraui: Iouis is omnia plena.
passages.english: They saw how absurd it would be if Jupiter were held to be the son of time, whom they either thought or wished to be thought an eternal god. But according to this new interpretation, which, if their ancients had had it, it would be a wonder had it escaped Cicero and Varro, they say that Jupiter is the son of Saturn as the spirit flowing forth from that supreme mind, which they wish to be, as it were, the soul of this world, filling all heavenly and earthly bodies. Hence that saying of Maro which I mentioned a little earlier: "All things are full of Jupiter."

passages.original: De deo Israhel respondeant, quem docere ista et iubere non tantum Christianorum, sed etiam Iudaeorum libri testantur, de ipso consulant deos suos, qui Christum blasphemari prohibuerunt, de deo Israhel, si audiant aliqua contumeliosa, respondeant. sed quos consulant? aut ubi iam consulant? libros suorum legant. si deum Israhel Iouem putant, sicut Varro scripsit, interim ut secundum eorum opinionem loquar, cur ergo Ioui non credunt idola esse delenda? si Saturnum putant, cur eum non colunt? aut cur non sic colunt, quemadmodum se coli per eos uates praecepit, per quos ea quae praedixit impleuit?
passages.english: Let them answer concerning the God of Israel, whom not only the books of the Christians but also those of the Jews testify teaches and commands these things; let them consult about him those gods of theirs who forbade Christ to be blasphemed; let them answer concerning the God of Israel, if they hear anything insulting [said of him]. But whom are they to consult? Or where can they consult now? Let them read the books of their own people. If they think the God of Israel is Jupiter, as Varro wrote, then (to speak for the moment according to their opinion) why do they not believe Jupiter that idols must be destroyed? If they think he is Saturn, why do they not worship him? Or why do they not worship him in the way he commanded himself to be worshipped through those prophets through whom he fulfilled the things he foretold?
passages.notes: The syntax of the opening sentence is loose; 'de ipso consulant deos suos' is taken as 'let them consult their gods about him'.

passages.original: quid aliud apertissime ostendens nisi illam scaenam esse tam turpem, ut tanto minus ibi homo esse debeat, quanto fuerit magis uir bonus? et tamen di eorum tali dedecore placabantur, quale a uiris bonis remouendum esse censebat. est etiam hinc eiusdem ipsius Ciceronis aperta confessio, ubi ait sibi Floram matrem ludorum celebritate placandam. in quibus ludis tanta exhiberi > turpitudo consueuit, ut in eorum conparatione ceteri honesti sint, a quibus tamen etiam ipsis agendis uiri boni prohibentur.
passages.english: What else was he showing most plainly but that the stage is so disgraceful that a man ought to be there all the less the better a man he is? And yet their gods were appeased by such disgrace as he judged should be kept away from good men. There is also on this point an open confession of the same Cicero, where he says that he must appease Flora the mother by the celebration of games. At these games such great obscenity was customarily exhibited that by comparison the rest are respectable, and yet good men are forbidden to take part even in performing those.
passages.notes: A stray '>' after 'exhiberi' in the source was ignored.
